NATIVE RUNTIME SECURITY / TECHNICAL PAPER

PHP2Shell

Technical Analysis of Memory Corruption Vulnerabilities in PHP

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619

Alwin @ LMS Securities

23 October 2026 · Static source & patch analysis

Download the paper (PDF) ↓
OOM corruption ↘Stale state ↘Patch analysis ↘

Abstract

PHP2Shell comprises CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, two classes of memory-safety failure in PHP’s native request-processing machinery. The first concerns allocation errors that interrupt operations after internal state becomes reachable but before initialization completes. The second concerns worker globals and shared metadata whose references outlive the validity of their backing request state or reservation. This study examines pinned PHP 8.5.11 and 8.5.12 implementation files, identifies the security commits on the 8.2 through 8.5 branches, and compares their actual changes with the PHP advisories and original research available by 23 October 2026. The analysis reconstructs hash-table insertion, automatic request parsing, upload-progress session decoding, fatal-error backtrace handling, and OPcache class-cache publication. It distinguishes same-request destruction of unfinished data, same-worker cross-request use-after-free, and cross-worker shared-state type confusion. Upstream and researcher publications establish unauthenticated code execution in demonstrated deployments and a separate worker-memory disclosure primitive; this study performs static analysis rather than independent exploitation. SAPI control flow materially changes reachability: mod_php cleans up failed startup, whereas PHP-FPM exits that child, although post-startup stale-state production remains relevant. The fixes replace unsafe immediate allocation-error interruption with delayed handling and hard process termination, move resets before early consumers, cover fast shutdown, and defer OPcache slot publication until its shared reservation is committed. The resulting evidence supports specific lifetime and publication corrections without establishing universal exploit portability or successful compromise from observed attack attempts alone.

Keywords: PHP; Zend Engine; out-of-memory handling; use-after-free; request lifecycle; OPcache; vulnerability analysis.

Author: Alwin @ LMS Securities. Research cutoff and retrieval date: 23 October 2026. Analysis: static source and patch review. All figures are original explanatory diagrams. No exploit payloads were developed or executed for this publication.

1 PHP2Shell vulnerability overview

1.1 Overview of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

The official advisories identify an OOM-corruption class, CVE-2026-109618, and a stale-global-state class, CVE-2026-109619. These identifiers describe related failures of native lifetime management, rather than one mandatory two-stage exploit. An allocation error can expose an unfinished object to cleanup within a request; an interrupted operation can also leave state for a later request. The analysis therefore follows the invalid state and its consumer, instead of treating the CVE number as a complete execution trace. [1, 2]

The evidence labels used throughout have specific meanings. CONFIRMED denotes directly inspected implementation or an explicit upstream statement. REPORTED denotes an attributed external demonstration or observation that was not independently reproduced here. INFERRED denotes a conclusion from the inspected control flow, with its prerequisites stated. UNVERIFIED denotes a question that available evidence does not settle. Confirmation of a source-level ordering is not confirmation of a working remote exploit. The accompanying ledger records these distinctions claim by claim.

Table 1 records the last preceding release inspected by comparison and the first fixed release in each maintained branch. The affected range is branch-specific: the notation does not mean that comparing an 8.2 version numerically with an 8.5 version determines susceptibility. Package vendors may incorporate a fix without changing the upstream base version. [3, 4]

Calif locates an early affected path in PHP 5.4.0; that historical floor is a researcher report, not a complete source audit of every historical release. The PHP announcement is dated 21 October, whereas the inspected 8.5.12 changelog entry says 22 October. Both dates are retained rather than silently reconciled. [3–5]

1.3 Vulnerability classification and severity

Both advisories publish a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, with the vector CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N. They list CWE-416, CWE-755, CWE-824, CWE-1325, and CWE-1419. These cover use-after-free, exceptional-condition handling, uninitialized pointers, allocation amplification, and incorrect initialization. High severity coexists with high attack complexity and present attack requirements; the score does not establish equal exploitability across SAPIs. [1, 2]

1.4 Attack prerequisites and confirmed security impact

Upstream confirms unauthenticated remote code execution with web-worker privileges. For the OOM CVE, mod_php has a demonstrated pre-application path; the advisory does not report a complete FPM exploit for that CVE. The stale-state advisory confirms a session-lifecycle FPM path subject to an appropriate application operation. Application authentication cannot intercept a parser that executes first, but application behavior can still determine whether a post-startup producer exists. [1, 2]

Amazon reports an exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry on 17 October 2026, before public disclosure, and further attempts around disclosure. Its report explicitly leaves success against real-world systems uncertain. This establishes observed attempts, not a measured population of compromised production servers. OpenAI’s publication supplies disclosure-coordination context; it is not used as proof of a particular memory primitive. [6, 7]

2 PHP memory management and request lifecycle

2.1 Zend Engine memory management

CONFIRMED. ZendMM distinguishes its reusable allocator machinery from the objects allocated through it. The inspected allocator manages chunks, small-allocation size classes, free slots, and larger allocations. A request can end while its worker and some allocator storage remain available for reuse. Consequently, the physical persistence of bytes does not extend the lifetime of a zend_string, HashTable, or decoder context that previously occupied them. [8, 9]

For this analysis, ownership means responsibility for preserving an object’s validity and eventually releasing it. A request-allocated value is valid only while the relevant allocation and its invariants remain live. A reference-count increment can preserve an object during ordinary request execution, but it does not turn a request allocation into independently persistent storage when the request heap is discarded. A worker-global pointer and the allocation it names must therefore be analyzed separately. This distinction is necessary to understand why merely resetting globals during the next normal RINIT can be too late. [10–12]

Two invariants organize the subsequent analysis. First, an object visible to destruction must contain valid discriminator, pointer, and ownership fields. Second, a reference that survives a lifetime boundary must either identify independently valid persistent storage or be invalidated before any consumer can use it. The bucket example violates the first. Session and decoder globals violate the second. OPcache adds a publication invariant: another worker must not observe an allocated slot until the shared reservation protects that slot from incompatible reuse. These are source-derived descriptions of the inspected mechanisms. [13–15]

2.2 PHP request initialization and shutdown

The relevant php_request_startup() ordering in PHP 8.5.11 is zend_activate(), sapi_activate(), php_hash_environment(), and zend_activate_modules(), followed by setting PG(modules_activated) true. Executor initialization and ordinary extension RINIT are different stages. It is therefore imprecise to say that upload parsing occurs before all PHP initialization: it occurs after executor activation but before ordinary module activation completes. [16]

sapi_activate() prepares request state and selects POST handling when automatic data reading is enabled and the method/content type qualify. php_hash_environment() activates the auto-globals; creating the POST auto-global can call the SAPI’s data handler. sapi_handle_post() dispatches the registered content-type parser. URL-encoded input reaches php_std_post_handler(), while multipart input reaches rfc1867_post_handler(). These are parser-selected paths, not a guarantee that every request triggers every handler. [17, 18]

The shutdown sequence explains the danger of partial startup. php_request_shutdown() conditionally invokes extension RSHUTDOWN using PG(modules_activated), destroys super-globals, deactivates executor/compiler state, performs extension and SAPI post-deactivation, and eventually shuts down the request memory manager. A false activation flag suppresses normal extension shutdown without suppressing every later heap-release operation. The lifetime of a published extension pointer cannot safely depend on an RSHUTDOWN that may never run. [16]

The SAPI decides whether that sequence is reached after startup failure. In Apache’s handler, failed request construction bails into an enclosing boundary; the subsequent top-level destructor calls request shutdown. In FPM’s main loop, startup failure finishes the FastCGI request, clears server context, shuts down the module, and returns FPM_EXIT_SOFTWARE. Reusing Apache’s cleanup argument for FPM would miss the latter’s process-exit boundary. [19, 20]

2.3 Out-of-memory handling and zend_bailout()

In the old allocator, zend_mm_safe_error() reports the memory-limit error within a protected region and then calls zend_bailout(). _zend_bailout() marks unclean shutdown, clears execution/compiler fields, and performs LONGJMP through the saved bailout address. This is a nonlocal transfer of C control flow. Statements between the interrupted allocation and the receiving boundary do not execute merely because they would have provided cleanup on an ordinary return. [8, 21]

OOM itself is resource exhaustion, not yet memory corruption. It becomes a memory-safety failure when the abrupt transfer leaves a reachable object whose invariants have not been restored and a later consumer trusts it. The allocation that triggers the transfer need not be the allocation containing the eventual invalid object. This explains why analyzing only the failed allocation’s return value is insufficient. The relevant transaction includes every state publication before the failure and every reachable consumer after it. [13, 16]

The patched policy is analyzed in Chapter 6. It does not erase nonlocal control flow from PHP. In particular, fatal errors other than OOM remain relevant to abandoned state, and the delayed handler itself can use a bailout at a controlled boundary when there is no userland frame to unwind. The implementation distinction is where invariants can be interrupted, not the mere presence of a jump primitive. [22, 23]

2.4 Request-local memory and persistent worker state

The families of state differ in both owner and consumer. Table 2 separates them so that a persistent pointer container is not mistaken for persistent referent storage. The repeated-request mechanisms concern the same surviving worker; the OPcache publication mechanism can involve another worker sharing cache metadata. [10, 11, 14, 24]

State Backing lifetime Surviving reference Relevant consumer
Partly initialized bucket Current request Counted table entry Request array destruction
Session ID/value Request heap Session globals Early upload-progress handling
Decoder bookkeeping Request heap BG(unserialize) Early nested-decoder initialization
Fatal backtrace Request heap Executor-global zval Diagnostic before executor reset
OPcache class-cache slot Shared metadata plus worker map Shared interned string offset Slot resolution in a worker

Table 2. Ownership and consumer map derived from inspected source. The OPcache row describes reservation/publication, rather than a freed Session object.

2.5 PHP session handling and OPcache internals

Upload progress is a native multipart callback registered by Session. The callback can initialize Session, update its progress record, and decode stored session data during automatic request processing. In the vulnerable version, the initial qualifying file event calls php_rinit_session(0) and publishes PS(id) before normal module RINIT. Update and cleanup functions invoke php_session_initialize(). This is why an application need not explicitly call session_start() for the early machinery to execute. [10, 25]

Session’s decoder uses the generic unserializer. php_var_unserialize_init() allocates a context on the request heap and, when appropriate, publishes it with a nonzero nesting level in Basic globals. A nested invocation reuses that context. php_var_unserialize_destroy() normally reverses the publication as nesting ends. The correctness of this pairing assumes that interruption cannot leave the published context visible after the heap containing it is gone. [11]

OPcache has a different architecture. Compiled structures and interned strings can be shared, while runtime pointer values are resolved through worker-local maps. ZEND_MAP_PTR_* macros distinguish direct pointers and offsets; CG(map_ptr_last) tracks a local allocation frontier. Persistence later copies that frontier to ZCSG(map_ptr_last). Publishing a shared string’s cache offset before updating the shared frontier exposes a reservation gap. That gap is an ordering problem even if the worker that made the change never handles another HTTP request. [14, 15]

3 CVE-2026-109618: Out-of-memory corruption

3.1 Root cause of incomplete initialization

CONFIRMED. _zend_hash_str_add_or_update_i() in PHP 8.5.11 first reserves the next mixed-table bucket by incrementing nNumUsed and nNumOfElements. It then obtains the bucket pointer and calls zend_string_init() to allocate its owned key. Hash, value, and chain metadata are assigned afterward. A memory-limit bailout at the key allocation abandons those assignments after the new bucket has already entered the range represented by the counters. [13]

The violated invariant concerns publication to traversal. nNumUsed is not just a future accounting value: destruction uses table metadata to decide which values it must inspect. At the interruption point, the newly counted region can still contain bytes from prior use of the backing allocation. Treating those bytes as a typed PHP value is invalid independently of whether they were deliberately influenced. Deliberate reuse can make the failure more useful, but it is an exploitation step beyond the ordering defect. [8, 13]

/* Original explanatory pseudocode: old insertion transaction. */
slot = publish_next_bucket(table);   /* traversal now includes slot */
key = allocate_owned_key(input);     /* old OOM path can jump away */
initialize_key_hash_value(slot, key, value);
complete_collision_metadata(table, slot);

Listing 1. Publication before fallible initialization. This is explanatory pseudocode, not a verbatim PHP excerpt or a usable exploit.

The request’s later array destruction supplies a consumer. A crash is one possible result, but a counted value can also influence reference-counted destruction and associated callbacks. Source inspection establishes invalid interpretation; code execution requires additional control over reclaimed data and valid addresses. No exact heap offsets, forged structures, or address-selection recipe is needed to establish the lifetime defect. [13, 16]

3.2 Allocation failures during HTTP request processing

The request path is concrete. Nested variable registration in php_register_variable_ex() can create an intermediate array and pass a string key to zend_symtable_str_update_ind(), which reaches string-key hash insertion. Automatic URL-encoded parsing can take this path through php_std_post_handler(). Multipart file metadata is also registered through the variable machinery. Therefore the vulnerable native transaction can run before execution of the requested PHP file. Different variable shapes can select different helpers; a statement that every scalar insertion has the same key-allocation window would be unjustified. [13, 18]

Multipart parsing provides several distinct forms of memory pressure. At handler entry, post_max_size is compared with SG(request_info).content_length. That guard constrains the declared length at that point. It is not, by itself, a proof that all decoded input streams and all native allocations are bounded identically. A frontend can impose additional limits, and a different POST reader can have a running-byte check. In particular, the inspected standard POST reader has its own consumed-byte logic; conclusions about the multipart handler should not be generalized to every reader. [17, 26]

multipart_buffer_headers() allocates header entries in a linked list. Their native representation adds pointer, entry, and allocation overhead beyond the transmitted header text. Separately, an empty file name marks the upload as absent and bypasses the temporary-file path that decrements upload_cnt; metadata registration still builds the file properties. Nested variable names add native tables and keys to those properties. These observations explain allocation amplification without assuming an unlimited multipart-part count or an unlimited accepted body. The source also maintains a body-part budget. [18, 26]

Calif’s published analysis identifies declared-length mismatches and empty-upload expansion as useful OOM routes. This corroborates the code’s distinction between transport-size controls and native allocation cost. The report does not establish that any particular reverse proxy forwards a lengthless or decompressed request in the required way; that condition belongs to deployment analysis. The defensive implication is limited: enforcing a body-size cap reduces pressure, but cannot alone prove absence of an interruptible allocation reachable through accepted input. [5, 26]

3.3 Upload-progress unserializer use-after-free

Wiz groups the upload-progress decoder UAF under CVE-2026-109618. Its underlying sequence also satisfies the stale-state pattern described by the second advisory. To preserve both the reported mapping and the implementation, this section treats OOM as a producer and a subsequent early decoder operation as the consumer. It does not reinterpret this case as a same-request bucket failure. [2, 27]

The old decoder publishes BG(unserialize).data and sets its nesting level when it allocates a fresh php_unserialize_data. Normal destruction decreases the level and clears the global pointer when the outer context ends. A fatal interruption between publication and destruction can leave a nonzero level with no valid live context. Basic’s ordinary RINIT clears serialization globals, but that RINIT follows automatic input processing. The next request can therefore reach upload-progress Session decoding before Basic gets its normal opportunity to reset them. [11, 12, 16]

At the later decoder entry, a nonzero level selects reuse rather than fresh allocation. Reuse is legitimate for genuine nested decoding within a live request; it is invalid when the global refers to a previous request’s released heap. Lists of reference entries and pending values then cease to be trusted bookkeeping. This establishes why stale decoder state can influence more than one later memory operation, without treating a corrupt list as an automatically complete RCE chain. [11]

The lifetime argument has four separate owners or roles: the worker owns the global container; the original request owns the context allocation; subsequent ordinary allocations may own reused storage; and the decoder is the mistaken consumer. A matching numeric address does not reconnect those ownership relations. The fix must therefore invalidate the publication before early decoding, rather than merely hope that a stale pointer is unlikely to be dereferenced. [11, 28]

3.4 Remote process-memory disclosure

The disclosed Session-ID mechanism has a different sink. PS(id) is a request-owned zend_string reference, published during early Session activity. If heap release occurs without the expected state reset, its value and length fields no longer describe an owned live string. In the inspected cookie function, php_session_send_cookie() calls php_url_encode() with ZSTR_VAL(PS(id)) and ZSTR_LEN(PS(id)), then appends the result to a Set-Cookie header. This is a concrete outbound data path, not just an invalid free. [10, 29]

Wiz reports that a later upload-progress cleanup can reach this state and return reclaimed worker memory in PHPSESSID; it reports unauthenticated disclosure of data beyond the attacker’s own request. Here, source review confirms the stale-state opportunity and string-to-cookie sink, while the complete remotely controlled disclosure remains REPORTED. Gates in session initialization, cookie policy, SAPI header handling, request affinity, and the contents of reclaimed storage still matter. [25, 27, 29]

A process-memory disclosure is not equivalent to reading arbitrary host memory. A PHP worker’s address space can contain data from other activity in that process, but it is not the address space of every other service or of the kernel. Nor does the available evidence establish a universally selectable read address and length on every build. The narrower consequence is already significant: exposed pointer-bearing data can reduce address uncertainty for a separate corruption primitive. [15, 29]

3.5 Memory corruption and demonstrated code-execution consequences

Datadog reports an independent laboratory RCE against PHP 8.5.11, commit 678778973bb4d4185c06ef1320de50f1a975d3c8, using Debian 12 ARM64 and Apache prefork/mod_php. Its detailed reproduction uses memory_limit=16M, post_max_size=64M, one worker, and disabled OPcache. Those choices aid observation and differ from the default-limit validation recorded upstream. The report also observes a successful response and continued worker operation; crashing the worker is not a necessary outcome. [30]

The three outcomes must be kept separate. Invalid bucket consumption is a source-confirmed violation. Worker-memory disclosure is a reported primitive with an identified native output sink. Remote code execution is externally demonstrated under stated conditions, not locally measured in this investigation. The paper does not extrapolate an exploit’s architecture, allocator layout, or address knowledge to every PHP deployment. The common technical fact is that request cleanup was allowed to interpret state whose initialization transaction had been abandoned. [13, 29, 30]

4 CVE-2026-109619: Stale global state

4.1 Request-owned memory retained in global state

The second class requires a publication that survives the loss of its referent. A producer need not be an OOM: any fatal transfer that bypasses the matching reset can matter, and late cleanup can publish new error state after an earlier reset. The important boundary is the point where PHP discards request allocations while the worker’s field remains accessible. A consumer then has to run before the next normal initialization replaces that field. The official advisory identifies both early diagnostics and upload progress as concrete consumer families. [2]

In the inspected Session callback, the first qualifying file event performs php_rinit_session(0), assigns a copied Session ID, and updates Session state. Ordinary multipart completion performs the matching cleanup. If the request aborts before completion while PG(modules_activated) is false, the normal extension shutdown gate also omits Session RSHUTDOWN. The request heap can still be released by the later shutdown sequence. This is a source-supported producer of request-owned Session references surviving in worker-global storage. [10, 16]

The resulting problem is not repaired by reference counting alone. The copied Session ID belongs to request-managed storage; the worker-global field is merely another reference to it. A subsequent request must treat that field as invalid once the backing request lifetime ends, regardless of whether the freed allocation happens to retain a plausible string header. For the decoder, the analogous invalidity involves a pointer plus nesting state, so clearing only the pointer or only the level would not express a clean empty context. [10, 11]

4.2 Cross-request use-after-free

The old callback separates its initial file event from its final completion event. A later upload-progress operation can reach cleanup without reproducing the exact file-start initialization that would have reset Session first. That separation makes it necessary to reason about event order, rather than assuming every multipart request begins by making Session globals safe. The relevant consumer may read a stale ID, initialize tracking over a stale Session value, or enter the generic decoder using stale Basic bookkeeping. These are related consumers, not a single guaranteed call sequence for every request. [10, 11, 25]

For a same-worker UAF, the required transition is: publish request-owned state; omit or bypass reset; release its allocation; retain the worker; then execute a consumer before reset. Removing any one step breaks that particular sequence. Heap reuse adds an exploitation condition by replacing the old referent with a new allocation whose bytes the consumer misinterprets. The ownership failure exists before an attacker obtains useful replacement bytes. [10–12]

FPM’s startup-failure exit removes the worker-retention step for an interrupted startup producer. It does not imply that all fatal errors after successful startup kill the worker. Calif reports a different FPM chain in which application execution publishes generic-decoder state, a fatal interruption abandons its cleanup, and a subsequent early upload-progress decode consumes it. The PHP stale-state advisory confirms an application-dependent FPM Session-lifecycle case. Thus, the correct FPM question is whether a reachable post-startup producer exists, followed by a suitable early consumer in that surviving child. [2, 5, 20]

This also explains why application-specific and application-independent statements can both be correct. The early consumer can exist below the application while the producer depends on an application route. Conversely, mod_php can supply both early production and later consumption without the requested script contributing useful behavior. The CVE labels do not remove this distinction. No inference about an arbitrary application’s decoding routes is made without inspecting that application’s code and configuration. [10, 19, 20]

4.3 Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free

The PHP 8.5 backtrace case is especially instructive because the inspected code qualifies a broad statement in the advisory. zend_error_zstr_at() clears the previous fatal backtrace and can populate EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace) when fatal backtraces are enabled. In zend_shutdown_executor_values(), the old backtrace destruction and ZVAL_UNDEF are inside if (!fast_shutdown). Under the ordinary nondebug ZendMM predicate, shutdown_executor() can select fast shutdown, leaving that reset unexecuted. The slow branch does contain a reset. It would therefore be inaccurate to say that the vulnerable source has no backtrace cleanup anywhere. [24, 31]

The security-relevant window precedes init_executor(), which normally undefines this field for the next request. Apache applies per-directory configuration before calling request startup. An invalid or deprecated setting can invoke diagnostic machinery in that earlier window. FPM’s init_request_info() similarly parses frontend-supplied PHP_VALUE and PHP_ADMIN_VALUE before startup, although such parameters and a diagnostic-producing setting are additional deployment conditions. Ordinary startup-only INI loading should not be conflated with a per-request consumer. [19, 20, 24]

The consumer does not need a visible error page. In zend_error_zstr_at(), clearing the previous backtrace already operates on the global before presentation decisions in the PHP error callback. The callback can also inspect backtrace state while composing error information. Changing display_errors, logging, or presentation severity does not establish that those native operations are skipped. The relevant protection is valid state at diagnostic entry. [31, 32]

Upstream identifies the fatal-backtrace case as a confirmed mod_php RCE path. Wiz reports a Drupal demonstration. Those statements establish an external exploit result, while the present source analysis establishes the field, the missed fast-shutdown reset, and the early diagnostic window. The inspection does not establish the same backtrace producer in PHP 8.2-8.4; their branch patch hunks appropriately do not add a reset for this PHP 8.5-specific field. [2, 27, 33–36]

4.4 OPcache shared-memory type confusion

The OPcache mechanism must be separated from same-worker request-heap UAF. In the vulnerable zend_accel_get_class_name_map_ptr(), an immutable permanent type-name string can immediately receive a newly allocated map-pointer offset and the class-cache flag. That string is visible through shared cache state. The local allocation frontier has advanced, but zend_accel_script_persist() updates ZCSG(map_ptr_last) only later in persistence. Shared visibility and shared reservation therefore occur at different moments. [14, 15]

If an interruption occurs after the string advertises the slot but before the shared frontier accounts for it, another worker can allocate that slot for a different purpose. Reading the old string then resolves an offset through a pointer-map entry with incompatible runtime meaning. This is a type-confusion argument: the same slot identity has been associated with different object interpretations. It does not require the shared string itself to have been freed, and terminating only the publishing worker does not by itself revoke metadata already visible to others. [14, 37]

The patch is particularly strong corroboration of this ordering. Its new pending-cache routines explicitly hold prospective string-slot assignments until after frontier publication, assert agreement between local and shared frontiers at commit, and discard an abandoned window. These changes address the visibility gap rather than merely clearing a request-global pointer. They also show why generic language such as ‘OPcache contains stale request data’ is insufficient to explain this case. [37, 38]

Wiz assigns this reported type-confusion RCE against WordPress to CVE-2026-109619. The inspected public evidence does not expose a complete build-by-build, configuration-by-configuration reliability matrix for that chain. Accordingly, shared publication and the defensive ordering are CONFIRMED, the incompatible-reuse consequence is INFERRED from those operations, and the remote code-execution demonstration remains REPORTED. OPcache must participate for this variant; the bucket and Session variants do not inherit that requirement. [14, 27, 37]

4.5 Memory corruption and demonstrated code-execution consequences

The native consumers have different effects. A stale Session ID can flow into response construction. A stale Session value or decoder context can be interpreted or destroyed as a live typed object. A stale backtrace can enter diagnostic destruction. A stale OPcache slot can resolve to the wrong runtime type. Their commonality is an invalid lifetime or publication assumption, not an identical corrupted structure, overwrite target, or heap layout. [11, 15, 29, 31]

The evidence supports a clear boundary between susceptibility and exploitation. Identifying a surviving field is not enough: a concrete producer, surviving lifetime, and consumer must be established. Identifying that sequence still does not prove address discovery, controlled reuse, or code execution on an untested build. Conversely, a confirmed default mod_php demonstration should not be discounted merely because a separately published laboratory setup uses different limits. Each result is evaluated against its own stated conditions. [2, 30]

5 Exploitation analysis

5.1 Exploitation through PHP request processing

PHP processes a qualifying body before it invokes the target script. Consequently, a parser-level path can expose a script whose entire application behavior is a harmless response. This is a property of the native call order, not an assumption that a CMS has an authentication defect. Apache’s post-catch request destructor is decisive for the unfinished-bucket startup case because it supplies the subsequent invalid-state consumer. Application middleware that starts later has no opportunity to restore a bucket whose native insertion already failed. [16, 18, 19]

The boundary differs for the application-dependent FPM lifecycle case. Startup must first succeed; an application or extension operation then has to publish state that a fatal error can leave behind. The later early consumer may again run before application authentication, but the producer’s reachability must be established for that application. A source-level candidate callback is not equivalent to an unauthenticated route that reliably reaches it. [5, 11, 20]

5.2 Memory reuse and the role of heap layout

Heap reuse converts an old reference into a reference to some new allocation at the same address. The original owner no longer controls the referent’s type or lifetime. In the bucket case, cleanup can encounter old bytes in an uninitialized region of a currently live backing allocation. In the decoder and Session cases, an entire pointed-to context may be dead. These are different reuse arrangements, so assumptions from one allocator size class or object representation cannot be transferred automatically to another primitive. [8, 11, 13]

Useful exploitation requires suitable replacement contents and sufficient knowledge of relevant addresses. A disclosure can assist address discovery, but it remains a separate primitive with its own worker-affinity and response-path conditions. ASLR, architecture, loaded extensions, allocator options, instrumentation, and existing cache state can change whether published assumptions hold. This is an analysis of the requirements implied by pointer-based interpretation, not a measurement of exploit success rates. [15, 24, 29]

Datadog’s detailed example demonstrates one concrete corruption-to-execution transition, rather than a universal set of memory offsets. Its published worker/process observations also show why a crash-only detector would be incomplete. This paper omits the forged native-object layout, target callback addresses, and command-execution construction. The defensively relevant finding is that a native destructor can receive an invalid typed value after unfinished insertion, and that deployment-specific layout determines how that error manifests. [13, 30]

5.3 Exploitability differences between Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM

Table 3 summarizes the SAPI boundary. ‘No complete exploit reported’ refers to the cited advisory and cutoff, and must not be read as a safety guarantee. ‘Source assessment’ means the named upstream assessment is available; this investigation did not retrieve FrankenPHP or LSAPI source trees. The php-cgi implementation was retrieved for context, but no end-to-end CGI exploitation claim was independently validated. [1–3, 39]

SAPI Supported conclusion Principal qualification
Apache mod_php Startup cleanup is source-confirmed; remote RCE is externally validated Request parsing and the relevant state/consumer must be enabled
PHP-FPM Failed startup exits child; post-startup stale-state path externally validated Suitable application producer and same-child consumer; no complete OOM-CVE exploit reported upstream
php-cgi / FastCGI Included in PHP’s affected web-runtime scope Process reuse and specific path require deployment review
FrankenPHP OOM startup-cleanup susceptibility assessed by upstream Not a locally audited implementation or demonstrated equivalent early INI consumer
LiteSpeed / LSAPI Upstream identifies conditional exposure Early configuration/application path and worker behavior require verification

Table 3. SAPI evidence and limitations, not a binary universal exploitability table.

Pool size changes opportunities for same-worker requests and allocation reuse; it does not reset an invalid pointer. Conversely, worker termination can remove one sequence entirely. These are not interchangeable statements. The FPM startup exit is a concrete control-flow break, whereas a larger worker pool leaves the failure present and changes scheduling uncertainty. Cross-worker OPcache publication requires a separate model because its incorrect shared metadata is not confined to a single retained request heap. [14, 19, 20]

5.4 Documented demonstrations involving WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla

Wiz’s published assignment is specific: the upload-progress decoder UAF was demonstrated against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla; fatal-backtrace UAF against Drupal; and OPcache type confusion against WordPress. It also reports application-agnostic disclosure. Those applications are demonstration targets, not a list of necessary vulnerable plugins. The report’s moving container tags are not immutable experiment identifiers, so this paper does not invent image digests or exact universal CMS configuration requirements. [27]

Calif describes a broader set of application demonstrations and a post-startup decoding path relevant to FPM. That report supports application-dependent reachability, but its broad statement about default configurations does not replace the per-SAPI conditions in the official advisories. Datadog’s separate 8.5.11 mod_php reproduction corroborates the bucket mechanism under its explicitly stated laboratory configuration. These are complementary observations with different scopes. [2, 5, 30]

5.5 Reliability, prerequisites, and environmental constraints

The critical constraints are the accepted input path, native memory amplification, interruption timing, worker survival, early consumer availability, and sufficiently controlled interpretation of reused data. The configuration matrix therefore records enabled features rather than merely a PHP version. A finite memory limit offers predictable pressure; removing that limit does not eliminate physical allocation failure. A disabled upload-progress feature removes the demonstrated early Session route but does not remove the bucket or backtrace mechanisms. [8, 11, 26, 31]

No quantitative reliability estimate is derived here. The public sources do not provide a common denominator of attempts, configurations, worker pools, and successful remote executions that could justify one. Amazon’s observed attempts also do not supply such a denominator. The supported result is narrower and auditable: specific native sequences are unsafe, several external exploit demonstrations exist, and the configurations that break one sequence cannot be assumed to break all of them. [1, 2, 6]

6 Patch analysis and remediation

6.1 Vulnerable PHP source-code analysis

The security changes were identified by their commit messages, not by attributing every release-to-release difference to PHP2Shell. Each of the following branch commits is titled Avoid state corruption via bailout and explicitly identifies both GHSA records. Their full patch files were inspected because GitHub’s comparison and commit JSON responses returned only 300 file entries, while the complete security patches contain more changed files. Using the truncated JSON alone would omit relevant changes and tests. [33–36]

Branch Security commit prefix Complete patch file count
8.2 01a40e89fbfc 389
8.3 3c832b523ee1 392
8.4 506e87fa7dcd 402
8.5 31c0ea7d7ff1 423

Table 4. Counts of diff --git file records in the downloaded security patches. They measure patch extent, not distinct vulnerabilities or independent experiments.

The main implementation comparison pins 8.5.11 at 678778973bb4d4185c06ef1320de50f1a975d3c8 and 8.5.12 at 136e049ac10b032c83018e65b63b6df858943750. Full tag resolutions for all four branches are recorded in Appendix A and the accompanying revision manifest. The analysis follows the security commit’s allocation, initialization, shutdown, Session, and OPcache changes separately from unrelated fixes shipped in the same releases. [13, 36, 40]

6.2 Changes to out-of-memory handling

The new allocator records pending OOM information and requests a VM interrupt instead of immediately abandoning an arbitrary non-fallible native allocation. zend_mm_check_limit() distinguishes a normal allocation from an explicitly fallible one. When soft-limit handling applies, the non-fallible operation may continue with real allocated storage, allowing its current transaction to restore invariants. A fallible operation can return failure for caller-directed cleanup. At the higher hard limit, the worker terminates. These are different policies; ‘allocation returns NULL everywhere’ would be an incorrect description. [9, 41]

zend_mm_delayed_verror() saves message/location information, marks OOM pending, and sets EG(vm_interrupt). The state machine distinguishes none, pending, handling, and handled. The VM’s interrupt helper checks pending OOM and calls zend_handle_delayed_oom(); function-call dispatch also observes the condition. The change makes delivery explicit at code boundaries where the engine can stop without treating unfinished native fields as completed objects. [9, 23, 41, 42]

Startup has no guarantee of reaching an application VM opcode, so the patch also instruments parsing and its return boundary. The URL-encoded reader checks pending OOM while accumulating and registering variables. Multipart processing adds checks around repeated work. After a POST handler returns, sapi_handle_post() releases its content-type copy and delivers pending OOM. Thus, the startup case is not explained adequately by saying only ‘wait for the next opcode’. [43–45]

zend_handle_delayed_oom() captures the current execution frame, marks handling in progress, and uses zend_throw_unwind_exit() when a frame exists. It reports the fatal condition under a protected boundary, restores execution-related bookkeeping, and releases saved OOM information. With no userland frame, it ultimately calls zend_bailout() to abort the request after handling. Therefore, the precise correction is removal of the unsafe immediate allocator bailout, not a global ban on bailout or longjmp. [22]

At the hard limit, zend_mm_hard_limit_error() prints a diagnostic and calls _exit(137), avoiding ordinary request destruction over potentially unfinished state. Physical allocation failure takes a distinct zend_out_of_memory() routine that prints a message and calls exit(1) in the inspected version. These exit functions should not be conflated. Neither path promises application shutdown callbacks or a successful HTTP response. [9, 46]

The default hard-limit buffer is also an implementation detail, not an unspecified infinite allowance. In 8.5.12, zend_mm_update_hard_limit() uses 200 percent through a 1 GiB soft limit and adds a fixed 1 GiB buffer for soft limits above 1 GiB, with saturation safeguards. The INI comment uses a broader boundary description, while the inspected condition is strictly greater than 1 GiB; both formulas coincide at exactly 1 GiB. The headroom supports completing transactions but does not remove denial-of-service considerations. [47, 48]

6.3 Persistent state cleanup and request lifecycle corrections

The Basic reset now runs early enough for its consumers. php_request_startup() invokes php_basic_early_rinit() immediately after zend_activate() and before sapi_activate(). The new routine clears serialization lock and serialization/unserialization bookkeeping and invokes the early URL-scanner reset. Basic’s normal RINIT alone could not protect the earlier upload-progress path. This is a direct movement of the initialization boundary relative to the consumer. [28, 48, 49]

Session also resets globals at MULTIPART_EVENT_START, before allocating the progress context. Its callback returns when modules are already activated, with an explicit comment about avoiding Session corruption through request_parse_body(). The update/cleanup helpers now check initialization success and active Session status instead of unconditionally treating initialization as successful. These changes address early entry and failure propagation, rather than assuming that a qualifying file-start event always precedes every consumer. [50]

Executor shutdown now undefines the fatal backtrace and resets error recording, recorded-error storage, error-handling mode, and exception state outside the old slow-shutdown branch. It also clears user handlers and their stacks on the fast path and resets object-store fields where fast cleanup discards storage. In main.c, super-global zvals are undefined after destruction, clear_last_error() runs immediately before memory-manager shutdown, and the module-activation flag is reset at the end. The late error reset covers state that post-deactivation diagnostics could repopulate after an earlier clear. [23, 48]

The Session patch includes additional isolation. Upload-progress decoding uses incomplete-class-only handling to avoid resolving classes or invoking application callbacks before ordinary module initialization. Corresponding serialization preserves the stored representation, while reserved bookkeeping-property collisions are rejected. This is more specific than setting an ordinary allowed-classes list: the new mode deliberately avoids class-resolution behavior at all. The two inspected Session regression tests target absence of user-code execution, preserved data, and reserved-property handling. [50–53]

These changes have different roles. Early Basic and Session resets directly break stale-state consumer sequences. Executor and late-error resets protect the worker boundary even after non-OOM fatal behavior. Incomplete-class-only decoding restricts pre-RINIT callback behavior. None should be described as the sole universal fix; they are complementary parts of the security change. That distinction matters when reviewing a downstream backport for completeness. [23, 28, 36, 50]

6.4 Source-code comparison before and after patching

The hash-table helper retains count-before-key ordering in 8.5.12. The central correction is therefore not a local reordering of those four lines. A soft-limit event no longer abruptly escapes that allocation point, and a hard-limit event terminates the worker rather than handing an unfinished bucket to ordinary request cleanup. The patch also introduces fallible APIs and OOM-aware callers across multiple subsystems. Describing the fix as ‘initialize the bucket before increasing the count’ would not match the inspected diff. [9, 36, 40]

/* Before: conceptual behavior of a non-fallible allocation. */
publish_partial_state();
allocate();              /* memory-limit failure: immediate bailout */
restore_invariant();     /* skipped */
/* ordinary cleanup may observe the partial publication */
/* After: conceptual behavior, below the hard limit. */
publish_partial_state();
allocate();              /* soft OOM recorded; allocation completes */
restore_invariant();
deliver_pending_oom_at_safe_boundary();
/* hard-limit failure instead terminates the worker */

Listings 2-3. Before/after control-flow comparison. Explicitly fallible allocations use a separate failure-return contract; these listings describe the non-fallible case.

OPcache receives its own transaction correction. zend_accel_pending_ce_cache_begin() creates a pending window and discards any abandoned predecessor. zend_accel_get_class_name_map_ptr() records prospective offsets in that window instead of immediately setting the shared string’s cache marker. After persistence, the code publishes ZCSG(map_ptr_last) and then calls the commit routine, which asserts frontier agreement before updating the strings. Post-deactivation discards an uncommitted window. [37, 38]

/* Original defensive pseudocode for shared-cache publication. */
begin_pending_cache_window();
persist_and_queue_prospective_slots();
publish_shared_frontier(local_frontier);
assert(shared_frontier == local_frontier);
commit_pending_string_references();
/* interrupted windows publish no queued string references */

Listing 4. OPcache reservation precedes shared reference publication. See Figure 5 for the corresponding visibility gap.

Across 8.2-8.5, the inspected patches preserve the same major strategy: delayed OOM, early Basic reset, early Session reset, broader executor cleanup, and pending OPcache publication. Branch differences follow available engine features. The PHP 8.5 patch adds the fatal-backtrace reset; the inspected earlier-branch hunks do not. The 8.2 OPcache persistence hunk publishes the ordinary frontier before commit, while 8.5 also updates its static frontier. This is evidence of branch adaptation, not evidence that all implementations are byte-identical. [33–36]

Regression coverage was inspected statically. The full patch contains tests for parsing under memory pressure and distinct soft/hard limits, as well as unserialization and interrupt cases. The inspected oom_error_get_last test checks that an exposed error message can outlive clearing error state; the decoder test exercises memory exhaustion in array unserialization; the interrupt test covers pending-OOM interaction with interrupts. The Session tests cover the pre-RINIT restriction. These are test intentions visible in source, not locally observed passes. No claim of running the upstream PHP test suite is made. [36, 52–56]

6.5 Fixed releases and limitations of temporary mitigations

Complete remediation requires the appropriate upstream fixed release or a vendor backport that includes the complete correction, followed by replacement or restart of workers still executing the old runtime. The fixed versions are 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. A CMS or Composer update is not proof that the native PHP interpreter was replaced; nor does a command-line version alone identify the runtime serving HTTP requests. [3, 4]

Temporary controls must be matched to a mechanism. Disabling upload progress removes its early Session route. On PHP 8.5, disabling fatal backtraces removes that producer. Administratively enforcing an unlimited PHP memory limit removes the predictable per-request threshold used in confirmed OOM chains, but does not guarantee that an underlying allocation cannot fail. Frontend limits, multipart restrictions, and worker lifetime restrictions can reduce opportunities without implementing the missing invariant. None is represented here as equivalent to the complete patch. [1, 2]

The source explains those limitations. A bucket failure does not depend on Session. A non-OOM fatal producer does not require crossing memory_limit. A diagnostic can consume state before display/log controls act. OPcache publication is not solved by merely restarting the worker that first published a slot. Remediation review must therefore cover allocation behavior, early initialization, shutdown cleanup, and shared publication rather than checking only one familiar configuration directive. [13, 23, 31, 37]

Conclusion

Pinned source inspection establishes two related failures of native transactional state. Old allocation-limit handling could abandon a counted hash-table entry before its fields were initialized. Separately, request-owned references could remain in worker globals until an early next-request consumer used them; OPcache exposed an analogous gap between publishing a slot reference and publishing its shared reservation. These mechanisms differ in object ownership, consumer timing, and worker scope.

The inspected security commits address those differences directly: defer soft OOM until controlled boundaries, terminate on the higher hard limit, reset state before early consumers and across fast shutdown, isolate pre-RINIT decoding, and publish OPcache references only after reservation. External publications establish concrete RCE and disclosure outcomes, while this work contributes an auditable static reconstruction and qualified comparison of their evidence. It does not claim independent remote exploitation, universal exploit reliability, or production compromise from telemetry describing attempts.

C. Evidence provenance and validation

All source retrievals took place on 23 October 2026. The source catalog contains nine official/research/telemetry publications, 38 pinned code locations, four identified security commits, and five individual regression-test sources. Several code locations share a source file; these counts are bibliographic entries, not independent corroborations. Retrieval hashes and byte counts accompany the local evidence. Full third-party report pages are not redistributed in the release archive; their URLs, retrieved metadata, and this work’s findings are preserved.

Code was reviewed statically. No PHP interpreter was built, no PHP exploit was executed, no internet target was probed, and no sanitizer result is claimed. Verification of the deliverables checks citation resolution, local assets, source identifiers, manuscript synchronization, PDF compilation/rendering, and browser behavior. Upstream tests were read for their defensive assertions, not reported as having passed locally. The README records actual validation results separately from suggested rebuild commands.

D. Unresolved technical questions

The public evidence does not establish immutable CMS image digests, a universal cross-SAPI reliability matrix, or independently verified real-world success for the MadPot attempts. No complete FPM OOM-CVE exploit is documented by the cited upstream advisory at the cutoff. FrankenPHP and LSAPI assessments rely on upstream descriptions rather than a local source checkout. Historical PHP 5.x susceptibility is reported rather than exhaustively re-audited. The 21/22 October release-date discrepancy is recorded without an inferred explanation. [1–6, 27]

Two apparent terminology conflicts are resolved only to the extent supported by code. First, the researcher grouping of OOM-produced Session/decoder cases overlaps the stale-state advisory; the paper preserves the reported CVE assignment while explicitly describing the cross-request lifecycle. Second, the backtrace advisory’s broad shutdown wording is narrowed by the observed slow-path reset and missing fast-path reset. Neither point is used to invent an additional CVE or to discount an established external exploit demonstration. [2, 24, 27]
